newsitem.title: INDIA: Yanni says India concerts to send message of unity.
newsitem.headline: Yanni says India concerts to send message of unity.

text.p: Greek-born composer Yanni wants a series of controversial concerts this week in front of India's Taj Mahal to send a message of unity across the world, and says the performances are not about money.
"I wanted to be one of the many people who wanted to stand up and send a message of unity," Yanni told Reuters in an interview late on Tuesday.
"I felt compelled that with the music that I write and also presenting it in front of the ultimate monument of love, the Taj Mahal, I think it will send a powerful message," he said.

The New Age composer's performances -- scheduled for Thursday, Friday and Saturday -- have sparked protests from conservationists, who say the government is neglecting the potential damage that the concerts can cause to the Taj Mahal.

India's Supreme Court recently dismissed two petitions against the concerts. The pleas said the light, sound and fuel emissions from the performances could damage the 17th-century white marble monument.
Last week five farmers threatened to set themselves on fire unless the government compensated them for crops destroyed in order to make way for a specially built stage for the concerts.
Organisers say the concerts' proceeds, estimated at up to $3 million, will go towards the preservation of the Taj Mahal. The 22,000 tickets on offer cost up to 10,000 rupees ($280) each.
"The concert is not about money. The money is a welcome by-product and it can be put to good use, but you cannot misplace the spirit of the concert," Yanni said.
"Originally, I wanted this concert to be a free concert," he said. "But it became necessary to limit the size of the audience to protect the monument."
The government of Uttar Pradesh state, where the Taj Mahal is located, and travel agents are rushing to cash in on the publicity generated by the concerts.

"People have travelled thousands of miles to see it. A million verses have been written about it. Soon, Yanni's exalted vibrations will surround it," said a state tourism department advertisment that exhorted people to visit the mausoleum built by a lovelorn Mughal emperor for a wife who died in childbirth.
The Press Trust of India said thousands of people had gathered outside the Taj on the bank of the River Yamuna as Yanni and his 47-piece orchestra rehearsed on Wednesday.

"His music may transpose you to the heavens but you'd need our de luxe fleet (of buses) to take you to his concerts," one travel agent's newspaper advertisement read. "For details, contact our Yanni desk."
